authors: Virginia L. Ma; Emmanuel J. Candes
title: Optimized Labeling Resource Allocation for Prediction-Assisted Inference via OPAL
what_it_holds: [from abstract only; HTML fetch was blocked] Active statistical inference setting. OPAL learns a labeling policy for individual data points, from a smooth parametric family, that converts a black-box model's uncertainty scores into labeling probabilities so as to minimise estimator variance, then runs inference on the collected labels. Tested on medical imaging (breast cancer subtype from histopathology, odds ratios across demographic groups), computational social science and proteomics. The abstract mentions no clusters, no cost per cluster or per unit, and no two-stage structure; what is allocated is labels across individual units, not clusters vs units per cluster.

authors: David Broska; Michael Howes
title: Cluster-Robust Prediction-Powered Inference
what_it_holds: [from abstract only] Cluster-Robust PPI++ gives closed-form standard errors under arbitrary within-cluster dependence, including partially labelled clusters (some units labelled, others not), which breaks PPI++ independence. States that it analyses how precision gains depend on the labeling design and derives a cluster-aware power tuning rule minimising asymptotic variance. The abstract does not mention cost per cluster vs per unit or an optimal number of units per cluster; this must be checked in the full text. Application: television news. Appears to be the nearest PPI-side paper to regimes A and B.

authors: Zikun Ye; Hema Yoganarasimhan
title: Rectification Difficulty and Optimal Sample Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys (earlier title seen: Adaptive Budget Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys)
what_it_holds: [read via alphaxiv summary page, not the PDF] Allocates human responses n_q across survey questions q under PPI++ with budget sum c_q n_q <= B (cost c_q per response) and weighted MSE objective. Closed form per the summary: n*_q = B sqrt(w_q A_q / c_q) / sum_j sqrt(w_j A_j c_j), described as a Neyman-type rule, where A_q is the question's rectification difficulty (variance left after the LLM prediction is used as control variate). More human responses go where the LLM leaves more residual uncertainty. Design-based/model-based status not stated. Clustering only appears in an extension (wave-level allocation in matrix sampling, sandwich covariance for within-respondent correlation, Web Appendix A.4). Residual-variance structure is analogous to C4 but allocated over tasks, not cluster size.

authors: Zikun Ye; Jiameng Lyu; Rui Tao
title: Allocating Human Oversight in AI-Enabled Analytics
what_it_holds: [from abstract only] Splits a human-validation budget B (cost c_q per label) across Q tasks using tuned PPI++. Each label also reveals the task's rectification difficulty (variance left after optimal use of the AI prediction as control variate). If difficulties were known a Neyman square-root rule is optimal; unknown ones are learned online by an upper-confidence-bound policy with vanishing efficiency loss against the oracle. No clusters or two-stage structure in the abstract.

authors: Pinaki Mohanty; Rajiv Khanna
title: Adaptive Stratified Active Statistical Inference (AdaStrat-ASI)
full_text_open: partial (workshop page and alphaxiv summary only)
what_it_holds: [from abstract/summary only] Labeling budget is split across strata, each stratum share proportional to its size times the square root of a difficulty score computed from the model and unlabeled data in a label-free scouting phase (Neyman-style), then stratum-specific sampling rules. Claims lower asymptotic variance than ASI. Strata are not clusters and no cost per stratum or per unit is described.

authors: Tom A. B. Snijders
title: Sampling (chapter in Multilevel Modelling of Health Statistics, ed. Leyland and Goldstein, Wiley 2001)
what_it_holds: [read through WebFetch summary, two passes] Section 7: cost c1 N + c2 N n, variance of form sigma1^2/N + sigma2^2/(N n), optimal cluster size n_opt = sqrt(c1 sigma2^2 / (c2 sigma1^2)) (eq. 12), independent of budget and of N; for a level-two covariate sigma1^2 = tau^2/s_X^2, sigma2^2 = sigma^2/s_X^2 so n_opt = sqrt(c1 sigma^2/(c2 tau^2)); for a pure level-one covariate with random intercept sigma1^2=0 so n_opt is infinite. Section 8 (eq. 13): residual variances (1-rho_W^2) sigma^2 and (1-rho_B^2) tau^2, and the factor tau^2 + sigma^2/n becomes (1-rho_B^2) tau^2 + (1-rho_W^2) sigma^2/n for a level-two variable. The chapter does not itself state that covariates change n_opt, so the plug-in of residual variances is implicit; it does not give the ratio form sqrt((1-R2_within)/rho_c). Model-based and design-based discussed.

authors: Mirjam Moerbeek; Gerard J. P. van Breukelen; Martijn P. F. Berger; Marlein Ausems
title: Optimal Sample Sizes in Experimental Designs With Individuals Nested Within Clusters
what_it_holds: [read via WebFetch summary] Cost c1 per individual, c2 per cluster, budget C. Optimal individuals per cluster n1 = sqrt[(c2 sigma_e^2)/(c1 sigma_u0^2)] = sqrt[(c2/c1)(1-rho)/rho]; clusters n2 = C/(c1 n1 + c2). Optimal n1 independent of budget. Covariates enter only through the variance components of the model, so they affect the optimum indirectly; no explicit residual-variance formula. Model-based, randomised experiments. (Their c1, c2 labels are the reverse of Snijders'.)

authors: Michael P. Cohen
title: Determining Sample Sizes for Surveys with Data Analyzed by Hierarchical Linear Models
what_it_holds: [read via WebFetch; formulas garbled in extraction, verify against original] Number of schools vs students per school under budget with cost per school Cs and per student Ck, q = school variance / student variance. Traditional survey optimum (cites Hansen et al. 1953) n_opt about sqrt(Cs/Ck) sqrt(1/q). Optimal n for estimating the school variance is at least sqrt2 times larger; for a student-level dummy coefficient the optimum is one school (impractical); school-level dummy gives the traditional value. No covariate-adjusted survey estimator.

authors: Nina Hagesaether; Li-Chun Zhang
title: A Note on the Effect of Auxiliary Information on the Variance of Cluster Sampling
what_it_holds: [read via WebFetch summary] Model-based synthesis of the design effect of cluster sampling, using anticipated variances. With auxiliary information the cluster-level GREG has no extra variance term for varying cluster sizes relative to element-level GREG, and the efficiency loss of clustering shrinks to the extent the conditional intra-cluster correlation given covariates is below the unconditional one. DEFF then depends on that conditional correlation and an average cluster size. No optimal cluster size or cost function is derived.

authors: Yiqun T. Chen; Moran Guo; Shengyi Li
title: Power Analysis for Prediction-Powered Inference
what_it_holds: [from abstract only] Closed-form power and sample-size formulas for PPI from the asymptotic variance; solves for the number of labelled samples n given unlabelled N. Rule of thumb: the reduction in required labelled samples relative to a classical design scales roughly with the R^2 between predictions and ground truth. Case studies include single-cell transcriptomics. No clusters, but the R^2 scaling is the analogue of the (1-R2_within) factor in C4.
